prime.problem: Most people start with Attention Is All You Need, and its Q, K and V float with nothing attached: the paper assumes you already know what a token is, where its vector comes from and how an answer comes out. This page lays out all ten stops in the order the data meets them, so each later card has a place to land.
prime.fits: The map for the course: read it first to see the route, or last as a recap. It builds on the hub's tokenizer and attention cards and points to the card and the paper for every stop.
expect: IDs → rows of the embedding table (7 × 896)
the block: positions, attention and feed-forward, run 24 times
logits → softmax → a decoder picks one token
the loop: append the token and run again
prime.goal: Name the ten stops in order, give the shape of the data between each pair, and say which card and which paper section teaches each stop.

attend: At which stops does the shape of the data change, and at which does it stay 7 × 896?
Why does the embedding table show up at two different stops?
Which stops hold weights, and why does the feed-forward part hold most of them?
Why is the loop (stop 10) a full trip round the route rather than a cheap extra step?
Which sections of Attention Is All You Need land on which stops, and what does it leave out?

must: The model only computes with numbers → text is cut into tokens and each token's ID picks a learned row → 29 characters become a 7 × 896 matrix before any block runs

Attention is the only stop where tokens read each other, and a weighted sum ignores order → position has to be written in (RoPE turns queries and keys) → the feed-forward part then works on each token alone and holds 63.5% of the weights
Only the last row is scored, against the same table as stop 3 → 151,936 scores → softmax gives a distribution and the decoder picks one token → the choice of decoder changes the answer you read
Each pass yields one token → the token is appended and the whole route runs again → 9 passes for our answer, whose probability is the product of its steps (about 0.11)
reference: Qwen2.5-0.5B's config: 24 layers, hidden size 896, 14 query heads, 2 key/value heads, FFN 4,864
the weight split: feed-forward 63.5%, embedding table 27.6%, attention 8.9%
the paper sections per stop listed in the table

compress.prompt: Close the page and draw the route as a snake of ten boxes. Label every arrow with the shape that passes along it, and under each box write the card that teaches it.
checklist: stops 4–6 as one block, 7 × 896 in and out, run 24 times
the decoder picks one token, and stop 10 appends it and runs again
the embedding table used at stop 3 and again at stop 7

retrieve.q: Explain why this course starts with the route and only then points to Attention Is All You Need.
answer: the paper's model sections cover stops 3–8 and assume tokens, decoding and the loop
with the route first, every stop has an input and output shape you can check
each paper then answers a question you already have, like where order goes back in

retrieve.q: Walk the question through the route and give the shape of the data after stops 2, 3, 6 and 7, and after the decoder.
answer: after stop 7: 151,936 scores from the last row
after the decoder: one token, which is appended for the next pass

retrieve.q: You have time to read one paper section before a week of debugging a model that writes repetitive answers. Pick a stop and a section from the table, and say what you skip by choosing it.
answer: repetition is a decoding problem: stops 8–9
read Holtzman et al. §3–4 and Table 1
you skip the block's internals, which don't cause the loop
if the repetition goes away with top-p, the decoder was the cause

compare.q: This map and the whole-route card both trace the same question. What does each one give you that the other doesn't?
answer: the route card traces the numbers at every stop and the answer token by token
the map adds the card and the paper sections for each stop, plus the weight split
use the route card to learn the mechanism, the map to plan what to read

compare.q: Zero to Hero builds a GPT bottom-up; this course follows data-flow order. How does the order change what you meet first, and when is each better?
answer: build order meets each piece when training needs it
data-flow order meets pieces in the order a trained model uses them
build order is better for writing a model; data-flow order for reading and debugging one

predict.q: Swap Qwen2.5-0.5B for a chat-tuned model of the same size and ask the same question. Which stops on the map change, and what happens to the first answer token's probability of 0.277? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: No stop changes: the route, the shapes and the decoder are the same. The weights differ, and a chat template wraps the question. The whole-route card says a chat model's template would make the first token near-certain. Our base model gives a hint: a plain Q/A wrapper already raised the first token to 0.797. The course didn't measure the chat model.

apply.task: Make the question twice as long, 14 tokens. Go through the ten stops and, for each, write whether its output shape changes and whether its number of weights changes.
apply.done: You have ten rows. Only the token count changes: 14 tokens, 14 × 896 through the blocks. The weights (494,032,768) and the 151,936 scores stay the same, and the decoder still picks one token.
apply.hint: Only stop 7 throws away rows: it scores the last one.
